title: ASCII: edge-routing engine crashes on dense fan-in graphs and misplaces fan-in/fan-out paths
author: dfadler
body:
## Summary The ASCII renderer's custom edge-routing/root-detection engine (`src/ascii/grid.ts`, `src/ascii/pathfinder.ts`, `src/ascii/edge-bundling.ts`) has several confirmed bugs ranging from hard crashes to misplaced/overlapping edge paths. Unlike the SVG path — which now uses ELK.js for layout — the ASCII renderer still uses the original custom layout/routing code, so these carry over unchanged from upstream. All five below were reproduced directly against this fork's current `main`. ### 1. Crash: `RangeError`/internal `Map maximum size exceeded` on dense fan-in graphs ```ts import { renderMermaidASCII } from 'zombie-mermaid' renderMermaidASCII(`graph TD A["AAA
(keita)"] --> C["CCC"] B["BBB
(yuriko)"] --> C C --> D["DDDD"] D --> E["EEEE"] A1["1 / 2"] --> A A2["3 / 4"] --> A A3["5 / 6"] --> A A4["XXX
(YYY ZZZ)"] --> A B1["77 77
(7 / 7 / 7)"] --> B B2["88-88
(99 99)"] --> B B3["111s 222s"] --> B D --> F{"F?"} F -->|Yes| G["High level
Tr"] F -->|No| H["Dumb Tr
S"]`) ``` On this fork, this call doesn't return within 60s and had to be force-killed — consistent with the reported unbounded blowup in `routeBundledEdges`/`getPath` in `src/ascii/pathfinder.ts` / `src/ascii/edge-bundling.ts`. ### 2. Crash: order-dependent root misdetection throws `Map maximum size exceeded` ```ts renderMermaidASCII(`graph TD A["Parent A"] --> C["Child C"] B["Parent B"] --> C C --> D["Grandchild D"] A1["Root 1"] --> A A2["Root 2"] --> A A3["Root 3"] --> A B1["Root 4"] --> B B2["Root 5"] --> B`) ``` Throws `Error: Map maximum size exceeded` on this fork. The root cause described upstream — `src/ascii/grid.ts`'s root-detection loop does a single forward pass over `graph.nodes` in Map-insertion order and misclassifies nodes as roots when `child → parent` edges appear after `parent → grandchild` edges in the source — still applies; here it manifests as a crash rather than just a flat/wrong layout, likely compounding with bug #1's pathfinding blowup once roots are misclassified. ### 3. Fan-in root nodes aren't grouped by target, causing overlapping edge paths ```ts renderMermaidASCII(`graph TD A1 --> A A2 --> A B1 --> B B2 --> B A --> C B --> C`) ``` Renders with A1/A2/B1/B2 on one flat row and their trunk edges visibly crossing/overlapping, instead of grouping each fan-in cluster (A1,A2 → A) contiguously and separately from (B1,B2 → B). Root cause: `createMapping` in `src/ascii/grid.ts` places root nodes sequentially with a fixed increment, without regard to which downstream target each root feeds into. ### 4. Sibling edges from the same source don't share a trunk segment ```ts renderMermaidASCII(`flowchart TB Src["Source"] Left["Left Target"] Center["Center Target"] Right["Right Target"] Src -->|left*| Left Src -->|center*| Center Src -->|right*| Right`) ``` The right-hand edge takes an unnecessary detour instead of sharing the horizontal trunk the other sibling edges use, per the upstream report. ### 5. Box-start connector (`├`/`┤`/`┬`/`┴`) drifts off the source box border when a sibling edge has a label ```ts renderMermaidASCII(`flowchart LR Src["Source"] Top["Top Target"] Mid["Middle Target"] Bot["Bottom Target"] Src -->|top*| Top Src -->|mid*| Mid Src -->|bot*| Bot`) ``` The `├` connector for the "Top" edge floats visibly right of `Source`'s actual right border once a sibling edge's label (`mid*`) widens that grid column — confirmed in this fork's output, matching the upstream repro almost exactly. ## Provenance Mined from an upstream audit of `lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid` open issues (tracking issue #21 in this repo). Based on upstream: - https://github.com/lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid/issues/64 (memory exhaustion) - https://github.com/lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid/issues/65 (order-dependent root detection) - https://github.com/lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid/issues/68 (fan-in grouping) - https://github.com/lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid/issues/111 (sibling trunk sharing) - https://github.com/lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid/issues/112 (box-start connector displacement) All five are bundled here because they live in the same small cluster of files (`src/ascii/grid.ts`, `pathfinder.ts`, `edge-bundling.ts`) and a fix likely touches shared root-detection/routing logic — but feel free to split into separate PRs.

comments.author: dfadler
comments.body: Cross-referencing the upstream PR audit (issue #22): item 1 (dense fan-in OOM crash) is fixed by PR #52 (porting lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid#66). Items 2 and 3 (order-dependent root misdetection, fan-in grouping) correspond to upstream lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid#67 and #69 by @ktrysmt — not ported yet; the diffs apply cleanly against this fork's `src/ascii/grid.ts` but change layout heuristics broadly enough (root placement order affects many of the ~63 ASCII golden-file snapshots) that they need careful visual review rather than a blind cherry-pick. Items 4 and 5 (sibling trunk sharing, box-start connector drift) correspond to upstream lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid#113 by @rmvegasm ("Fixes #111 Fixes #112"), not yet reviewed in depth.

title: ASCII erDiagram: stray connector glyphs, edges routed through boxes, and large blank gutters
author: aahoughton
body:
**Environment:** `zombie-mermaid@1.5.0`, Node v24.14.0, `renderMermaidASCII(src)` (Unicode mode, no options).

Filed separately from the label-overwrite corruption
(see *ASCII erDiagram: relationship labels are composited over entity boxes*),
since these are visible layout defects rather than silent data loss. Splitting them
so neither half gets lost — lukilabs/beautiful-mermaid#121 bundled several ASCII symptoms and only
some were addressed.

## 1. Stray vertical connector next to the cardinality glyph

Visible in the smallest possible diagram:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    CUSTOMER ||--o{ ORDER : places
```

```
┌──────────┐        ┌───────┐    
│ CUSTOMER │─│───○╟─│ ORDER │    
└──────────┘ places └───────┘    
                                 
                                 
```

The connector renders as `─│───○╟─`. The `│` immediately after the `CUSTOMER`
border is not part of either cardinality notation — `||` (exactly one) and `o{`
(zero or more) are already represented by `╟` and `○`. On vertical runs the same
artifact appears doubled, as `││` and `○╟│`.

## 2. Edges route through entity boxes

In multi-entity layouts, edge paths are drawn straight across box interiors rather
than routed around them, and vertical segments cut through horizontal edge labels —
producing labels split by a line, e.g. `appear│_in`.

## 3. Disconnected entities get a large blank gutter

```mermaid
erDiagram
    CUSTOMER ||--o{ ORDER : places
    PRODUCT ||--o{ LINE_ITEM : appears_in
```

```
┌──────────┐        ┌───────┐           
│ CUSTOMER │─│───○╟─│ ORDER │           
└──────────┘ places └───────┘           
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                        
                                        
┌─────────┐            ┌───────────┐    
│ PRODUCT │─│───────○╟─│ LINE_ITEM │    
└─────────┘ appears_in └───────────┘    
                                        
                                        
```

Entities in separate components are separated by a run of blank rows rather than
packed, which for a schema with a few unrelated tables leaves most of the output
empty.

## Note

The SVG backend renders all of these correctly — correct routing, labels sitting on
their edges, no overlap. These are ASCII-backend-only.

title: Scope a pluggable/domain-aware layout architecture
author: dfadler
body:
🤖 **Claude:** Split from #536.

## Context

Competing tools treat layout as a swappable subsystem rather than one hardcoded algorithm: D2 exposes three interchangeable engines (Dagre, ELK, TALA — the last purpose-built for architecture diagrams), and even ELK's "Graphviz Dot" option is a literal wrapper around the external `dot` binary rather than a native reimplementation. Separately, academic work is moving toward layout that preserves a diagram's intrinsic order (e.g. keeping a control-flow graph's execution order top-to-bottom) instead of applying generic layered layout everywhere.

## Task

Assess whether zombie-mermaid's current renderer can support either of:

- swapping in an alternate layout engine per diagram type, or
- domain-aware layout for specific diagram types (e.g. sequence/flowchart execution order)

without a from-scratch layout rewrite. Produce a short feasibility note: what's retrofittable, what isn't, and roughly what a from-scratch path would look like if one is needed.

## References

- https://d2lang.com/tour/layouts/
- https://eclipse.dev/elk/reference/algorithms/org-eclipse-elk-graphviz-dot.html
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.05066 (CFG-aware layout research)

Note: a related claim that SPX (a multi-objective layout optimizer) beats dot/dagre/OGDF on all tested DAGs was checked and refuted during the original research pass — don't treat SPX as proven-best, only as "optimizes multiple criteria jointly."

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.author: dfadler
comments.body:
🤖 **Claude:** Full scoping analysis for #578 (the TL;DR now lives in
`docs/decisions/layout-architecture-scoping.md`, trimmed down per
[review feedback](https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/pull/578#discussion_r3950308772)
to keep the committed doc short and put the detailed notes here instead).

## Current architecture, as read

### SVG side: three independent ELK integrations, not one seam

`src/layout-engine.ts` is the only diagram family with a real pipeline
separation:

```
MermaidGraph --[to-elk.ts: mermaidToElk()]--> ElkNode (ELK JSON)
            --[elk-instance.ts: elkLayoutSync()]--> ElkNode (positioned)
            --[from-elk.ts: elkToPositioned()]--> PositionedGraph
```

This looks like a clean seam — `mermaidToElk` / `elkToPositioned` bookend a
pure `elkLayoutSync(graph)` call — but the seam is at the wrong altitude for
swapping the *engine*: `mermaidToElk` returns an `ElkNode`, not a neutral
graph. Its 700+ lines are almost entirely ELK-specific: `elk.algorithm`,
`elk.direction`, `elk.hierarchyHandling` (`SEPARATE` vs `INCLUDE_CHILDREN`),
hand-built hierarchical ports and hop/bridge edges to route cross-subgraph
edges under `SEPARATE` (`src/layout-engine/to-elk.ts:320-405`), and per-edge
`elk.edgeLabels.inline`/`placement` options. None of this could be handed to
a different engine (Dagre, or a native `dot` binary) without a full rewrite
of the conversion — the subgraph/port/hop-edge decomposition exists
specifically to work around ELK's own hierarchy-handling semantics
(`to-elk.ts:320-329`'s comment explains this is required because "ELK only
resolves an edge automatically when both endpoints are visible from the
edge's container").

Worse, `class/layout.ts` and `er/layout.ts` **do not go through
`layout-engine.ts` at all.** Each imports `elkLayoutSync` from
`elk-instance.ts` directly and builds its own inline `ElkNode` graph:

- `src/class/layout.ts:191-195` constructs its own root `ElkNode` with
  `'elk.algorithm': 'layered'`, `'elk.direction': 'DOWN'` hardcoded (no
  direction-override or subgraph support at all — class diagrams have no
  subgraphs).
- `src/er/layout.ts` does the same, with its own `directionToElk()` — a
  near-duplicate of `to-elk.ts`'s function of the same name, but with a
  different default (`RIGHT` vs flowchart's `DOWN`) baked in independently.

The only code shared across all three ELK call sites is
`src/layout-engine/elk-adapter-utils.ts`, whose own header comment states the
problem plainly: *"`from-elk.ts` (flowchart/state), `src/class/layout.ts`,
and `src/er/layout.ts` each independently walk an ELK edge's
`section.startPoint → bendPoints → endPoint` into a `Point[]`... This module
is the single place that logic lives, so the three call sites can't drift."*
That module only covers point/label extraction from ELK's *output* — none of
the graph-*construction* logic is shared. Three separate teams of code build
three separate `ElkNode` graphs, using ELK-specific vocabulary throughout.

**What a real engine-swap seam would need**: an engine-neutral intermediate
graph type (nodes with size/shape metadata, edges with optional labels,
compound/subgraph nesting, a requested direction) that all three diagram
types build once, plus a per-engine adapter (`toElk(graph)`, `toDagre(graph)`,
etc.) that translates *that* into the target engine's format, mirroring what
D2 does (see the D2 comparison below: D2 keeps one graph model and
per-engine "shims" for the handful of features an engine can't express, e.g.
container width/height only working on ELK/TALA). That's a from-scratch
design task, not a refactor of the existing conversion code — `to-elk.ts`
and its siblings would need to be rewritten against the new neutral type
rather than adapted, since so much of their logic (hop-edge decomposition,
hierarchical ports) exists purely to satisfy ELK's own `hierarchyHandling`
quirks and has no equivalent in a neutral model.

### SVG side: two diagram types that don't use graph layout at all

- `src/sequence/layout.ts` never touches ELK. Its header comment says so
  explicitly: *"Custom timeline-based layout (no ELK — sequence diagrams
  aren't graphs)."* Actors get fixed X positions by declaration order;
  messages are stacked at `messageY` strictly in **source/chronological
  order** (`layoutSequenceDiagram`, `src/sequence/layout.ts:351-478` — the
  main loop advances `messageY` monotonically per message, block, and note,
  with no reordering or crossing-minimization pass at all).
- `src/xychart/layout.ts` is direct coordinate-space math for axes/bars/
  lines — not a node/edge graph, so "layout engine" doesn't apply.

### ASCII side: four more independent layout algorithms, none of them ELK

None of the ASCII renderers reuse the SVG-side `PositionedGraph`/ELK
pipeline or the SVG-side per-diagram-type layout modules:

- `src/ascii/converter.ts` + `src/ascii/grid.ts`: a from-scratch
  character-grid layout for flowcharts/state diagrams (rank/column
  assignment, subgraph bounding boxes, its own `getEffectiveDirection`,
  its own edge routing in `edge-routing.ts`/`pathfinder.ts`). No ELK
  import anywhere in `src/ascii/`.
- `src/ascii/class-diagram.ts`: its own row-packing layout
  (`currentX`/`currentY` slot placement, `src/ascii/class-diagram.ts:462-500`)
  — completely independent of `src/class/layout.ts`'s ELK-based SVG layout.
  Parses the diagram fresh from `class/parser.ts` rather than reusing any
  positioned output.
- `src/ascii/er-diagram.ts`: its own layout (`findConnectedComponents`,
  `chooseFreeRow`) — independent of `src/er/layout.ts`.
- `src/ascii/sequence.ts`: its own position computation
  (`renderSequenceAscii`) — independent of `src/sequence/layout.ts`, though
  it's a much smaller reimplementation since sequence layout is already
  simple (chronological stacking) on both sides.

Net effect: **there are roughly nine distinct layout implementations** in
this codebase (SVG flowchart/state, SVG class, SVG ER, SVG sequence, SVG
xychart, ASCII flowchart/state, ASCII class, ASCII ER, ASCII sequence), and
only the SVG flowchart/state one uses a general-purpose layout algorithm at
all (ELK). Any "pluggable layout engine" framing that starts from "swap ELK
for X" only ever addresses 3 of those 9 — and even within those 3, ELK isn't
behind one seam.

## D2's layout abstraction

Per [d2lang.com/tour/layouts](https://d2lang.com/tour/layouts/), D2 keeps a
single internal graph model and lets the user pick the rendering engine at
the CLI/config level (`--layout=dagre|elk|tala`, or `$D2_LAYOUT`). The three
engines aren't drop-in equivalent, though — D2's own docs list per-engine
capability gaps (container-to-child connections fail under Dagre;
width/height constraints on containers only work under ELK/TALA;
position-locking is TALA-only), which D2 handles as documented
engine-specific limitations rather than papering over them. That's the
realistic bar for "pluggable": not perfect parity across engines, but one
shared graph model with engine-specific adapters and known, documented
capability gaps per engine — not, as zombie-mermaid has today, the target
engine's own types doing double duty as the internal model in three
independently-written places.

ELK's own "Graphviz Dot" algorithm option
([reference](https://eclipse.dev/elk/reference/algorithms/org-eclipse-elk-graphviz-dot.html))
reinforces the same point from the other direction: ELK itself is built as a
pluggable-algorithm framework (15+ algorithms, including one that wraps
Graphviz's layered approach), all consumed through one shared `elk.*`
layout-option vocabulary and one `ElkNode` I/O format. zombie-mermaid
currently gets zero benefit from that pluggability — the codebase always
requests `'elk.algorithm': 'layered'` and never varies it — but it's a
reminder that "swap the algorithm" and "swap the engine" are different asks:
ELK already supports the former cheaply (change one string, in three
places), while the latter is the expensive one this note is about.

## Domain-aware layout assessment

Sequence diagrams are, today, already the thing the issue speculates might
be "feasible as an incremental addition": their layout preserves message
order top-to-bottom by construction, because the layout was never written as
a general graph algorithm in the first place (`sequence/layout.ts`'s own
header: "Custom timeline-based layout (no ELK — sequence diagrams aren't
graphs)"). This wasn't a deliberate response to order-preservation research —
it's the natural shape of a sequence diagram's semantics (messages *are* a
timeline) — but it validates the same idea the VEIL paper
(arXiv:2511.05066) argues for CFGs: skip generic layered/Sugiyama layout
entirely when the diagram already carries an intrinsic order, and position
directly from that order instead of asking a crossing-minimizing algorithm
to (hopefully) preserve it as a side effect.

Flowcharts get a much weaker version of the same idea:
`to-elk.ts:294`'s `'elk.layered.considerModelOrder.strategy':
'NODES_AND_EDGES'` asks ELK to use declaration order as a *tie-break* during
crossing minimization (confirmed load-bearing by the sibling-subgraph
reversal logic just above it, `to-elk.ts:425-448`, needed specifically
because "ELK's `considerModelOrder` uses [model order] as a tie-break during
crossing minimization and thus what ultimately decides left-right sibling
order" — see issue #444). That's meaningfully different from sequence
diagrams' guarantee: it's a heuristic nudge inside a general algorithm, not a
structural property of the layout. A flowchart with a strong top-to-bottom
"execution order" reading (state diagrams are the most CFG-like diagram type
this repo renders) could in principle get closer to VEIL's approach, but
that would mean **replacing** ELK's layered algorithm for that diagram type
with a bespoke order-preserving placement pass — the same category of
from-scratch work as building a new engine adapter, not a tweak to existing
ELK options. It is not a "comparatively low-risk near-term win": it would be
a new, unproven layout algorithm competing with a mature one (ELK layered),
for a diagram type (state/flowchart) that currently has zero user-reported
complaints about node ordering in this repo's issue history searched during
this scoping pass.

**No specific near-term win is being called out.** The honest read is that
sequence diagrams already capture the easy, high-value case for free, and
extending true order-preservation to flowchart/state diagrams is
architecturally the same size of effort as the engine-swap problem above
(a new layout algorithm needs to be designed and validated against the
existing ELK-based rendering across the diagram-heavy test/visual-regression
suite), not a smaller, separable one.

## What a from-scratch path would look like (if pursued later)

1. Design one engine-neutral graph IR (nodes with size + shape metadata,
   edges with optional labels, compound/nesting, requested direction) —
   informed by, but not copied from, `MermaidGraph` (which is closer to the
   parser's AST than a layout-ready graph) and ELK's own `ElkNode` shape
   (which is the right *shape* but the wrong *vocabulary* to keep neutral).
2. Rewrite `to-elk.ts`, `class/layout.ts`'s graph-building half, and
   `er/layout.ts`'s graph-building half to each build the neutral IR once,
   sharing that construction code instead of duplicating it (this alone —
   independent of any engine swap — would close the three-way duplication
   flagged above; tracked separately as #616).
3. Add an `elk` adapter (`neutralToElk`, mostly today's `to-elk.ts` logic
   moved one layer down) and, only once a second engine is actually wanted,
   a second adapter for it, following D2's precedent of documenting
   per-engine capability gaps rather than requiring full parity.
4. Leave ASCII layout untouched — it is not graph-algorithm-driven in any
   diagram type today, so it sits outside this seam entirely regardless of
   what happens on the SVG side.

This is scoping only — no estimate is given here for calendar cost, since
the point of this note is the shape of the problem, not a commitment to do
it.

title: ASCII: two edges between the same pair of nodes in *opposite* directions still corrupt each other's labels and lose an arrowhead (the reverse-direction half of #329)
author: theimpostor
body:
## Summary

In a left-to-right flowchart, a pair of edges running both ways between the same
two nodes is drawn as a single arrow. The two labels are composited onto the same
cells, producing garbled text, and one of the two arrowheads is dropped.

[#329](https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/issues/329) reported this for two
edges in the **same** direction, and that case is now fixed — 2.1.0 gives the two
edges separate lanes and renders both labels in full. The **opposite**-direction
case still produces the exact output #329 quoted, character for character,
including the `SFirst─Arrow` corruption.

The SVG backend renders the same source correctly. Only `renderMermaidASCII` is
affected.

## Version

- `zombie-mermaid` 2.1.0 (latest on npm)
- Bun 1.4.2, macOS 26 (Darwin 25.6.0), arm64
- Also reproduces on 1.7.0 and on `beautiful-mermaid` 1.1.3 with byte-identical
  output, so this is longstanding rather than a recent regression

## Minimal reproduction

Two nodes, two labelled edges, opposite directions.

```mermaid
graph LR
  Browser -- request --> Server
  Server -- response --> Browser
```

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
mkdir zm-repro && cd zm-repro
bun init -y
bun add zombie-mermaid@2.1.0
```

Save as `repro.ts`:

```ts
import { renderMermaidASCII } from "zombie-mermaid";

const source = `graph LR
  Browser -- request --> Server
  Server -- response --> Browser`;

console.log(renderMermaidASCII(source, { colorMode: "none" }));
```

Then:

```bash
bun repro.ts
```

No options beyond `colorMode` are needed. The failure also occurs with
`useAscii: true` and at any `paddingX`.

## Actual output

```text
┌─────────┐          ┌────────┐
│         │          │        │
│ Browser ├rrequest─►┤ Server │
│         │          │        │
└─────────┘          └────────┘
```

Three defects are visible:

1. `request` and `response` are composited into `rrequest`. The `r` of `response`
   lands on the cell before the `r` of `request`. No reader can recover either
   word.
2. One arrowhead is drawn, not two. The edge reads as one-way.
3. The two edges occupy one row, so nothing indicates the source declared two.

## Expected output

Either two lanes, as the same-direction case now produces, or the merged
bidirectional form the renderer already draws correctly when asked for it
explicitly:

```text
┌─────────┐                  ┌────────┐
│         │                  │        │
│ Browser ◄request/response─►│ Server │
│         │                  │        │
└─────────┘                  └────────┘
```

## The same-direction case is already fixed

For contrast, #329's own source on 2.1.0:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A -->|First Arrow| B
    A -->|Second Arrow| B
```

```text
┌───┐              ┌───┐
│   │              │   │
│ A ├─First─Arrow─►│ B │
│   │              ▲   │
└───┤              ├───┘
    │              │
    └Second─Arrow──┘
```

Correct: two lanes, both labels intact, both arrowheads. Now reverse the second
edge, changing nothing else:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A -->|First Arrow| B
    B -->|Second Arrow| A
```

```text
┌───┐              ┌───┐
│   │              │   │
│ A ├SFirst─Arrow─►┤ B │
│   │              │   │
└───┘              └───┘
```

This is byte-identical to the "Actual output" block in #329. Whatever gave the
same-direction pair its own lanes is not reached when the second edge points the
other way.

## Trigger conditions

Each case was tested independently against 2.1.0.

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `graph LR`, both edges labelled | **Reproduces** — labels garbled, one arrowhead |
| `graph RL`, both edges labelled | **Reproduces** — identical output to LR |
| `graph LR`, only the forward edge labelled | **Reproduces** — reverse arrowhead silently lost |
| `graph LR`, only the reverse edge labelled | **Reproduces** — reverse arrowhead silently lost |
| `graph LR`, neither edge labelled | OK — renders `◄►`, both arrowheads |
| `graph LR`, explicit `A <-->\|request/response\| B` | OK |
| `graph TB` / `graph TD`, both edges labelled | OK — labels stacked, both arrowheads |
| `graph LR`, self loop `A -- loop --> A` | OK |
| `graph LR`, chain of two opposed pairs | **Reproduces** — see below |

Two rows are worth calling out.

**Labels cause the lost arrowhead.** The unlabelled pair renders `│ A ├◄►┤ B │`
with both arrowheads. Adding a label to just one of the two edges removes the
other edge's arrowhead:

```text
graph LR              ┌───┐      ┌───┐
  A -- ping --> B     │ A ├ping─►┤ B │
  B --> A             └───┘      └───┘
```

So the renderer can draw the bidirectional connector. Label placement is what
suppresses it.

**A chain loses whole edges.** Four edges, two opposed pairs:

```mermaid
graph LR
  A -- a1 --> B
  B -- b1 --> A
  B -- b2 --> C
  C -- c1 --> B
```

```text
┌───┐    ┌───┐    ┌───┐
│   │    │   │    │   │
│ A ├a1─►┤ B ├b2─►┤ C │
│   │    │   │    │   │
└───┘    └───┘    └───┘
```

`b1` and `c1` are gone, along with both reverse directions. The output reads as a
one-way pipeline `A → B → C`. Nothing marks the loss.

## The SVG backend is correct

`renderMermaidSVG` on the same source emits both labels, well separated, and two
arrowheads:

```html
<text x="206.225" y="50.15"  text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" ...>request</text>
<text x="201.830" y="83.450" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" ...>response</text>
```

Two `marker-end` attributes are present. The labels are 33.3 px apart vertically
at an 11 px font size, so they do not collide. The defect is confined to the
ASCII backend.

## Impact

Request/response, client/server, publish/acknowledge, read/write — a labelled
round trip between two components is one of the most common shapes in an
architecture diagram, and `graph LR` is the natural direction to draw it in.

The output is not merely ugly. It states something false. A round trip is shown
as one-way, and in the chain case two edges disappear from the drawing entirely.
A reader cannot tell, because the result is a well-formed box drawing. A caller
cannot detect it either, because `renderMermaidASCII` does not throw.

The workaround is to rewrite the source before rendering, folding each opposed
pair into one `A <-->|x/y| B` statement. That works — it produces the "Expected
output" above — but it needs a full parse of the source, an exact-match rewrite,
and a re-parse to verify the rewrite changed nothing else, because it is only
safe when the fold is provably equivalent. It also discards which label belongs
to which direction, which the source stated and the drawing can no longer say.

## Note

#329 closed against the same-direction case, and
[#532](https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/issues/532) proposes unifying
ASCII collision avoidance into one occupancy module. If the lane assignment that
fixed #329 keys on the ordered pair `(source, target)` rather than the unordered
pair, the reverse edge would land in a different group and never be offset. That
would be consistent with everything above, including why the unlabelled case
still finds its bidirectional form. It may be worth folding this into #532's
scope rather than patching the ordered-pair grouping in place.

title: Flowchart: long routed edges cross subgraph titles and share one trunk (CI/CD, git branching)
author: dfadler
body:
Two flowchart samples render with **long routed edges that cross a subgraph title or share a single trunk**, so it is hard to see which edge goes where. In both, the official Mermaid layout is much cleaner. Found during a fidelity review of the SVG visual baselines against official mermaid.js 11.17.2 (while regenerating them in #1229). I confirmed both against the reference myself. This is layout quality, not wrong information. ## 1. CI/CD pipeline: the `No` edge crosses the "CI Pipeline" title ```mermaid graph TD subgraph ci [CI Pipeline] A[Push Code] --> B{Tests Pass?} B -->|Yes| C[Build Image] B -->|No| D[Fix & Retry] D -.-> A end C --> E([Deploy Staging]) E --> F{QA Approved?} F -->|Yes| G((Production)) F -->|No| D ```
official Mermaid 11.17.2zombie-mermaid
The layout is inverted compared with the reference (`Deploy Staging` at the top, the subgraph below). The `QA Approved?` `No` edge runs down into the subgraph, crosses the "CI Pipeline" title and the full height of the box to reach `Fix & Retry`, and `Build Image` to `Deploy Staging` is routed out the bottom, around the right and back up, hugging the subgraph border. ## 2. Git branching: several edges share one vertical trunk ```mermaid graph LR A[main] --> B[develop] B --> C[feature/auth] B --> D[feature/ui] C --> E{PR Review} D --> E E -->|approved| B B --> F[release/1.0] F --> G{Tests?} G -->|pass| A G -->|fail| F ```
official Mermaid 11.17.2zombie-mermaid
The edges from `develop` to `feature/auth`, `feature/ui` and `release/1.0` and the arrows into and out of `Tests?` overlap on one vertical trunk next to `develop`; the `approved` arrow lands on the right edge of `develop`, and `fail` enters `release/1.0` at the same spot as the trunk. Direction and endpoints are ambiguous. ## Not part of this issue The `Source` to `Input` edge crossing the "Processing Pipeline" title in "Flowchart: Subgraph Direction Override" (`general-18`) is **also in official Mermaid's render**, so it is inherent to the layout and not tracked here. ## Affected samples `packages/site/samples-data.ts`: "Flowchart: CI/CD Pipeline" (`general-21`) and "Flowchart: Git Branching Workflow" (`general-24`). ## Where to look (hypothesis, not debugged) Layout goes through ELK (`packages/svg-renderer/src/layout-engine/to-elk.ts`, `from-elk.ts`). The subgraph case likely involves how edges that cross a compound node are routed; the trunk case, how parallel edges from one node are separated. ## Acceptance Decide what is acceptable. A reasonable bar: no edge passes through a subgraph title, and edges leaving one node in different directions do not overlap. The affected baselines regenerated afterwards. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: State diagram: inverted or hard-to-follow layout in the basic and connection-lifecycle samples
author: dfadler
body:
Two state-diagram samples render with a **hard-to-follow layout** compared with official Mermaid: the diagram runs bottom-to-top, the start marker is beside a state instead of above the chain, and parallel edges between the same states are hard to tell apart. The information is present; the reading order is not. Found during a fidelity review of the SVG visual baselines against official mermaid.js 11.17.2 (while regenerating them in #1229). I confirmed both against the reference myself. ## 1. Basic state diagram ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Idle Idle --> Active : start Active --> Idle : cancel Active --> Done : complete Done --> [*] ```
official Mermaid 11.17.2zombie-mermaid
`Active` sits above `Idle`, so `Idle --> Active` runs upward; the `[*]` start dot is to the right of `Idle`, entering from the right; the `start` and `cancel` edges run side by side and are hard to tell apart; `Done` sits off to the right. ## 2. Connection lifecycle ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Closed Closed --> Connecting : connect Connecting --> Connected : success Connecting --> Closed : timeout Connected --> Disconnecting : close Connected --> Reconnecting : error Reconnecting --> Connected : success Reconnecting --> Closed : max_retries Disconnecting --> Closed : done Closed --> [*] ```
official Mermaid 11.17.2zombie-mermaid
The layout is inverted: `Closed` is at the bottom with the `[*]` start dot beside it (bottom right) and its arrow pointing down into `Closed`, so it reads like another incoming edge; the end marker is below `Closed`. Long edges run up the left side to `Connecting` and `Reconnecting`, and several verticals converge on `Closed` and `Connected` (`success`, `error`, `success`, `close`), so it is hard to tell which label belongs to which edge or that `error` and `success` run in opposite directions between `Connected` and `Reconnecting`. ## Affected samples `packages/site/samples-data.ts`: "State: Basic State Diagram" (`general-29`) and "State: Connection Lifecycle" (`general-31`). The other state samples (composite states, CJK names) were not flagged. ## Where to look (hypothesis, not debugged) State diagrams share the ELK-based layout engine (`packages/svg-renderer/src/layout-engine/`). Layers seem to be assigned so the start state does not end up first; check how `[*]` start and end nodes are constrained (a start node pinned to the first layer and an end node to the last) and the cycle handling for back-edges such as `Active --> Idle`. ## Acceptance The start marker is at the beginning of the reading direction and the end marker at its end, and back-edges (`cancel`, `error`) do not reverse the main chain. The affected baselines regenerated afterwards. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Class diagram: disconnected components are not laid out in source order (SVG)
author: dfadler
body:
## Problem

In a class diagram made of several disconnected components, zombie-mermaid's SVG output does not lay them out in source order. Official Mermaid places each component left to right in the order it is declared; ours reorders them and wraps onto a second row.

Found while verifying #1247 (the `*--` / `o--` marker fix). It is not caused by that PR: the "before" render there has the same order.

## Repro

```mermaid
classDiagram
  A <|-- B : inheritance
  C *-- D : composition
  E o-- F : aggregation
  G --> H : association
  I ..> J : dependency
  K ..|> L : realization
```

Expected order (official Mermaid): A/B, C/D, E/F, G/H, I/J, K/L, left to right in one row.

Ours renders the first row as K/L, A/B, G/H, E/F and a second row as C/D, I/J.

| official Mermaid | zombie-mermaid |
| --- | --- |
| ![reference: source order](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1fbcb090-057c-4fe9-bc12-a3539e3352c8) | ![zombie-mermaid: K A G E / C I](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a1ec56b0-b2ec-4dee-90df-9bfb1e759ec7) |

## Where to look (hypothesis, not debugged)

`packages/svg-renderer/src/class/layout.ts`: disconnected components appear to be ordered by something other than declaration order (graph or rank order) before being packed into rows. Mermaid keeps declaration order.

## Affected samples

"Class: All 6 Relationship Types" (`general-60`) for sure; likely any class sample with more than one disconnected component.

## Acceptance

- Disconnected components are placed in source order.
- A test that asserts the order of the positioned components (the visual suite alone would not make the intent clear).
- SVG baselines for the affected samples regenerated (Linux and darwin). Expect a lot of PNG churn, which is why this is separate from #1247.

title: State diagrams: apply reading-order layout to composite states
author: dfadler
body:
Follow-up to #1240 / #1280. That PR lays flat state diagrams out in reading order (`MODEL_ORDER` cycle breaking, start marker pinned `FIRST`, end marker `LAST_SEPARATE`, `postCompaction: NONE`), but deliberately does not apply those options to diagrams with composite states.

## Problem
Applying the same ELK options to composite states flipped the `general-30` sample (State: Composite States). Subgraph (composite) nodes are added to the ELK model after the leaf nodes, so under `MODEL_ORDER` a composite is treated as coming after every leaf and the layer order inverts.

## Proposed fix
Rework the ELK model order in `packages/svg-renderer/src/layout-engine/to-elk.ts` so a composite state sits at its first-mention position among its siblings, then apply the flat-state options to composite diagrams too. Related: #1239 hits the same ordering limitation for flowchart subgraphs (a comment in `to-elk.ts` says the reorder was avoided for blast radius).

## Acceptance
- `general-30` (and other composite state samples) read in source order, start marker first and end marker last.
- Reviewed before/after for every sample whose baseline changes.

title: ascii: back edges and rank-skipping edges take long wrap-around detours
author: dfadler
body:
## Problem

Edges that must go around other nodes (back edges such as `C→A` and `D→A`, or edges that skip a rank like `A→D`) take long detours around the far side of the diagram, with many bends, and end far from where the edge starts. Both ends and the route are hard to follow, and several detours run next to each other.

Repro (see #1345 real-terminal capture):

```mermaid
graph TD
A -->|x| B
B -->|long label| A
A -->|long label| C
C -->|ab| A
B -->|mid| D
A -->|ab| D
D -->|x| A
```

Examples: `C→A` leaves C's right side, climbs past the top of A and re-enters A from the right with a `◄`; `D→A` enters D's right side after a staircase of bends.

## Expected

Mermaid/dagre routes a back edge as a smooth path on the near side of the nodes it connects, with the arrowhead on the target's border facing the direction of travel. In ASCII: prefer the shortest route with the fewest bends, keep a back edge on the same side as its source/target where it can, and avoid wrapping around the whole diagram when a nearer lane exists.

title: ASCII: labelled fan-in labels collide when the child also fans out (onetwo)
author: dfadler
body:
## Problem

A node with two labelled parents that also fans out to two or more children renders its parents' labels on top of each other:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    X -->|one| A
    Y -->|two| A
    A --> B
    A --> C
```

In ASCII output the labels `one` and `two` collide and read as `onetwo`, so one label is effectively lost.

## Cause (as found while working #1339)

#1340 (`centerParentsOverChildren`) centres `A` over its children but does not set `node.fanInCentered`. The per-edge side-entry routing added for labelled fan-in (#1344, on top of #1346) keys off that flag, so it never applies here, and both labelled edges still share one horizontal run and the final drop.

## Possible fix

Set `fanInCentered` when `centerParentsOverChildren` moves a node that has several labelled parents, so the side-entry route is used. Needs the same gates as `labeledFanInFits` (not LR, no cycle through a parent).

## Notes

- Found by the agent working #1344 on main (post-#1340). It was reproduced through `renderMermaidASCII`, not a real-terminal capture, and I have not re-checked it against current main after #1344 merged; a real-terminal repro should come first.
- Related: #1339.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD

    D --> F
    F --> G
```

A larger graph with the same shape throws with different fractional coordinates, for example `segment from (3.75,9) to (1,9)`.

title: ASCII: with `paddingX` 2 or less, an LR fan-in edge stops beside the child's border with no junction or arrowhead
author: theimpostor
body:
## Summary

In 4.2.1, LR fan-in routes each parent through its right face and joins the edges in the gap before the child (#1346). When `paddingX` is 1 or 2, the gap is too narrow for the join. The edge from the farther parent rises in the gap and stops one row under the other edge. It does not join that edge and has no arrowhead. With `paddingX: 3`, the same graph is correct.

## Reproduction

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A --> B
  A --> C
  B --> C
```

```ts
import { renderMermaidASCII } from "zombie-mermaid/ascii";

console.log(renderMermaidASCII(source, { colorMode: "none", paddingX: 2 }));
```

## Actual (4.2.1, `paddingX: 2`)

```text
┌───┐  ┌───┐  ┌───┐
│   │  │   │  │   │
│ A ├─►│ B ├─►│ C │
│   │ ││   │ ││   │
└───┘ │└───┘ │└───┘
      │      │
      └──────┘
```

The `A → C` edge leaves A at the bottom of the gap and runs under B. Then it rises beside C's left border and stops. It has no `┬` junction with `B → C` and no arrowhead. The same column also touches B's left border, so the edge looks like it ends at B.

`paddingX: 1` shows the same problem:

```text
┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐
│   │ │   │ │   │
│ A ├►│ B ├►│ C │
│   │││   │││   │
└───┘│└───┘│└───┘
     │     │
     └─────┘
```

## Correct with `paddingX: 3`

```text
┌───┐   ┌───┐   ┌───┐
│   │   │   │   │   │
│ A ├─┬►│ B ├─┬►│ C │
│   │ │ │   │ │ │   │
└───┘ │ └───┘ │ └───┘
      │       │
      └───────┘
```

## Expected

With a narrow `paddingX`, the fan-in either joins the other edge with a junction, or the renderer falls back to the 4.1.0 layout. In 4.1.0 with `paddingX: 2`, C sits under B and `A → C` enters C's left side with its own arrowhead.

In larger diagrams, the same defect occurs at multi-line nodes. For example, the stroke leaves from a lower port of a two-line node, such as `├─┐`.

## Environment

- zombie-mermaid 4.2.1 and 4.2.0 (4.1.0 is correct with `paddingX` 1 and 2)
- Bun 1.4.2, macOS arm64

title: ascii LR: edges sharing a lane into one node can't be told apart, so labels can't be attributed
author: dfadler
body:
## Problem

In an LR flowchart, several edges into the same node can be routed onto one shared lane and one shared final drop. The ASCII output then no longer matches the Mermaid source: four separate edges look like one path, and a reader cannot tell which label belongs to which edge.

#1433, #1448, #1463 and #1464 each stopped labels from erasing a stroke or each other. That makes the text readable, but it cannot fix this: with four edges on one path, moving labels around only moves the ambiguity.

## Repro

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A --> B
  A -->|first| C
  B -->|second| C
  A -->|third| D
  C -->|fourth| D
  B -->|fifth| D
  B -->|sixth| D
  A -->|seventh| D
```

In Mermaid (SVG) `B → D` (`fifth`, `sixth`) and `A → D` (`third`, `seventh`) are four separate edges with their own paths and labels.

## Actual (ASCII, after #1464)

```
┌───┐     ┌───┐         ┌───┐        ┌───┐
│   │     │   │ second  │   │fourth  │   │
│ A ├──┬─►│ B ├────┬───►│ C ├────┬──►│ D │
│   │  │  │   │    │    │   │  fifth │   │
└─┬─┘  │  └─┬─┘  first  └───┘  third └───┘
  │    │    │      │       sixth │     ▲
  └────┴────┴──────┴─────────────┴─────┘
                    seventh
```

- All four edges share the bottom lane and the single drop into D.
- `fifth` and `third` stack on the same stem; `sixth` sits on the lane. Nothing ties a label to its edge.
- `seventh` hangs under the lane, far from the edge it names.

## Expected

An edge that is a separate edge in the source stays distinguishable in the ASCII, or, where edges are deliberately bundled, a label can be attributed to its edge (for example one lane or drop per edge, or a bundle drawn so each label is attached to a visible branch).

## Notes

- Label placement alone cannot fix this: the ambiguity comes from the router merging the edges onto one path. The fix is in edge routing/bundling (`edge-routing.ts`, `draw-bundles.ts`, `edge-bundling.ts` are the likely places), so it needs its own change and review across other diagrams.
- Not measured: how many existing samples would change if lanes were split, or how bundling currently decides to merge these edges. That is the first thing to find out.
- Related: #1413 (label-vs-label overlap), #1463 (`sixtfifth`, fixed in #1464).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.author: dfadler
comments.body:
🤖 **Claude:**

## Measurement results

Full notes and method: [research doc @ 6356973](https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/blob/6356973b59eec3149fe56073b6e944b97a43cc29/docs/research/1467-ascii-lr-shared-lane-measurement.md) (PR #1476, docs only, no renderer change).

### How the edges end up merged
- It is not bundling. `analyzeEdgeBundles` returns `[]` for non-TD, so no edge in the repro has `edge.bundle` set and `draw-bundles.ts` is not involved.
- It comes from A\*. `determinePath` calls `getPath` per edge with a uniform step cost of 1. Only node boxes are obstacles, and drawn edges are neither obstacles nor penalised. Edges with the same target and equal-length routes therefore pick the same cells: the same under-row lane and the same final drop.
- Only same-source-and-target edges get separate lanes, via `assignParallelEdgeLanes`. `A->D`, `B->D` and `C->D` are not a parallel group, so nothing separates them.

### Blast radius
I counted edge pairs with the same target (or source) that share 2 or more cells, across the 29 flowchart samples and the repro:
- 2 of 29 samples have any shared run. CI/CD Pipeline (TD) has one both-labeled fan-in pair that reads fine. Git Branching Workflow (LR) has one unlabeled fan-out pair.
- Neither sample shows the unattributable-label symptom. Only the repro does, with 4 fan-in pairs, all both-labeled.
- This is an upper bound, since any shared run counts. I did not scan other diagram types or the unit-test corpus.

### Options with this evidence
- **(a) one lane/drop per source edge:** needs an edge-occupancy cost in `getPath` or a per-target port allocator. It changes the layout of every fan-in graph, LR and TD. The effect on the samples is small, but the code surface is large.
- **(b) keep the shared path, attribute labels:** local to label placement and drawing. It cannot make 4 stacked edges distinguishable on its own.
- **(c) middle path:** split lanes only when a shared run carries 2 or more labeled edges. This touches none of the current samples except the repro.

### Open
The test corpus and real-world graphs are unmeasured, so a refresh is needed before choosing (a) or (c). This issue stays open for the choice between the options.

comments.author: dfadler
comments.body:
🤖 **Claude:** Closing note, written after the fact (see #1557). #1486 and #1489 together shipped option (c) for LR: once a labeled edge shares a bent run with an earlier labeled edge into the same node, it gets its own lane. In the repro, `third`, `fifth`, `sixth` and `seventh` now each sit on their own lane.

Not shipped: option (a). The lanes still merge into one final drop into D, `first` and `third` share a run out of A, the first two labeled edges into a node may still share a run on purpose, and TD and unlabeled edges are unchanged.

If the shared final drop matters for your diagrams, say so and we will open a separate issue for it. Thanks for the report.

title: Investigate 'Labeled Fan-In (LR)' and four weaker flowcharts against Mermaid side by side
author: dfadler
body:
## Context
`layout:oracle` (official mermaid 11.17.2) shows 17% vertical agreement for the flowchart "Labeled Fan-In (LR)" (horizontal 100%); other flowcharts are 90-100%. Four more are weaker, vertical/horizontal: CI/CD Pipeline 95/76, Git Branching Workflow 95/86, System Architecture 96/93, Decision Tree 90/95. All have subgraphs or fan-out. Unconfirmed: bug or intentional-but-undocumented.

## Source
Found in the 2026-10-10 project review (#1502). Snapshot fidelity audit (#1592), findings 1-2.

## Open questions / proposed work
- Compare "Labeled Fan-In (LR)" and the four weaker flowcharts against Mermaid side by side.
- Refresh baselines only after that investigation.

comments.author: dfadler
comments.body:
## Side-by-side investigation (read-only; no code, snapshot or baseline touched)

Method: each sample rendered through `renderMermaidSVG` (ours) and through mermaid 11.17.2 in headless Chromium (`scripts/lib/real-mermaid.ts`, what `layout:oracle` uses); I viewed every image, and compared node positions from `layoutFlowchartSync` against the browser-measured mermaid SVG. The ELK cross-axis option sweep from [#1700](https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/issues/1700#issuecomment-6102501427) is not repeated.

**Headline: in all five cases both renderers assign the same layers and the same node order within each layer, except Labeled Fan-In (a mirrored tie-break) and Decision Tree (one sink node lands a layer late). The scores come from cross-axis placement and edge routing, not from structural disagreement.**

### 1. Labeled Fan-In (LR), 17% vertical

| mermaid | ours |
|---|---|
| ![c0-mermaid](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/58a9c7c3-f13d-4332-92ad-7ef83da0705c) | ![c0-ours](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2c016f81-53cd-4f9f-a517-9f62209902d4) |

Layers match (A | B | C | D). Within the A/B/C columns the vertical order is mirrored: mermaid has C above A above B (B at y=138, C at y=64); ours has B above A above C (B y=66, C y=123). Crossing counts look equal, so this is a symmetric tie that dagre and ELK break in opposite directions (ELK follows source order top-to-bottom via `considerModelOrder.strategy: NODES_AND_EDGES`, `to-elk.ts`; dagre's LR ordering is reversed). With only 4 nodes, one flipped pair swings the percentage hugely. Both drawings are valid; ours also reads better (one lane per edge, labels on their stroke, per #1467).
**Class: intentional tie-break difference (model order), not a bug.** No decision doc states it; the code comment on `considerModelOrder` is the closest. **Recommendation:** no renderer change; document it in `docs/layout-fidelity-scorecard.md` (or exclude this sample from the headline mean) and refresh nothing.

### 2. CI/CD Pipeline, 95% vertical / 76% horizontal

| mermaid | ours |
|---|---|
| ![c1-mermaid](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bbd57587-8678-4eb4-be47-11ec6c3c8b05) | ![c1-ours](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a3b935f0-ad0b-4412-bf4f-b5ed0a11fe5d) |

Same layers and same topology. Differences: mermaid keeps Deploy Staging, QA Approved? and Production in one column and draws one "Yes" edge straight down; ours pushes Production left of the diamond's centre because the two diamond exits (Yes/No) take separate ports. Ours also routes the dashed Fix-to-Push back-edge inside the subgraph; mermaid does the same. This is the BK node-placement/port effect already measured in #1700 (every ELK option rejected).
**Class: intentional trade-off (cross-axis placement; cited: #1700, #1312).** **Recommendation:** no change; a bespoke post-layout column-alignment pass is the only fix and is a separate design decision.

### 3. Git Branching Workflow, 95% vertical / 86% horizontal

| mermaid | ours |
|---|---|
| ![c2-mermaid](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d4f3f92a-e106-4fb6-a330-25994e3ca68e) | ![c2-ours](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/45aa5f7c-4373-45a0-a7a4-91c6a5fdfde5) |

Same five layers and same order. Only offsets differ: mermaid puts `Tests?` (G) below `release/1.0` (G y=309 vs F y=268); ours puts it slightly above (G y=199 vs F y=219) because ELK centres it against its two back-edge endpoints. Back-edge labels pass/fail/approved sit sensibly in both.
**Class: Mermaid/ELK placement quirk, cosmetic.** **Recommendation:** none.

### 4. System Architecture, 96% vertical / 93% horizontal

| mermaid | ours |
|---|---|
| ![c3-mermaid](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e8d56f64-bbf4-4602-9a1e-e976aa558443) | ![c3-ours](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ada500ec-7368-4b86-aa48-d05384fcac0c) |

Same layers, same order, same subgraph containment. Score gap is cross-axis offsets (ours packs Web/Mobile App tighter and centres the Client Layer box differently). One real visual defect in ours worth noting: the three edges leaving API Gateway share a vertical trunk that runs exactly along the right border of the Client Layer box, so the border and the connector overlap; mermaid clips each edge separately. Related prior art: `docs/decisions/cluster-exit-anchoring-scoping-1135.md` (ASCII side only).
**Class: scoring gap is intentional/ELK; the trunk-on-border is a small bug candidate (SVG edge routing at subgraph boundary).** **Recommendation:** file a separate low-priority issue for the trunk overlap; do not touch baselines for the scores.

### 5. Decision Tree, 90% vertical / 95% horizontal

| mermaid | ours |
|---|---|
| ![c4-mermaid](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/85301143-841f-458b-9663-b612343707ae) | ![c4-ours](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ead363b3-696f-4051-8917-bd126445ecde) |

This is the one case with a real layer difference. Mermaid puts `Go outside` (C) in the same layer as `Have umbrella?`; ours places it a layer lower, giving `Is it raining? -> No -> Go outside` a long vertical edge, and `Go with umbrella` (D) likewise sits in its own row between `Is it heavy?` and the last row (mermaid: D beside E). Measured with the sample source: with edge labels removed C's top is 361 and B spans 232-398 (same layer); with the labels C top is 498 and B spans 300-466 (C one layer later). So the late sinks are triggered by labeled edges (ELK's inline-centred label layers give the layering free slack for a leaf with a single in-edge), not by the shape sizes.
**Class: bug (cosmetic layering), caused by our label handling plus ELK's default network-simplex slack for sink nodes.** No decision doc or comment calls it intentional. **Recommendation:** worth a follow-up issue: try pinning single-in-edge sink nodes to their parent's next layer (or `layering.strategy`/`nodePromotion`), measure with `layout:oracle` over all 27 samples, as #1700 did for placement. `layering.*` was not in #1700's sweep, so this is not a repeat.

| Case | Class | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Labeled Fan-In (LR) | intentional tie-break (model order) | document; no baseline refresh |
| CI/CD Pipeline | intentional trade-off (#1700) | none |
| Git Branching | ELK/Mermaid placement quirk | none |
| System Architecture | scores intentional; trunk on subgraph border is a small bug | file separate issue |
| Decision Tree | bug: sink node one layer late when edges are labeled | file follow-up on layering |

title: svg: Decision Tree sink node lands one layer late when edges are labeled (differs from mermaid.js)
author: dfadler
body:
## Problem

In the "Decision Tree" gallery sample, adding edge labels pushes a sink node one layer later than without labels, which disagrees with mermaid.js.

From the investigation, in the SVG output on `main`: with the labels present, `Go outside` (`C`) lands one layer below `Have umbrella?` (`B`); mermaid.js puts them in the same layer. Removing the labels from the source puts `C` back beside `B`. Edge labels are the trigger, not node shapes.

This sample scores 90% vertical and 95% horizontal in `pnpm run layout:oracle`, among the weaker flowcharts.

## Where to look (cause not verified)

The cause has not been confirmed. One possibility is that labeled edges take up extra space in the layered layout and shift the sink down, while mermaid.js/dagre accounts for labels differently; that is a guess. The ELK options we pass are set in `packages/svg-renderer/src/layout-engine/to-elk.ts`. The earlier ELK alignment sweep on #1700 covered node-placement options, not layering options.

## Suggested work

1. Reproduce with the sample's source, with and without labels, and confirm the extra layer.
2. Try layering strategy or label placement options, scoring every flowchart with `pnpm run layout:oracle` before and after. Reject any change that lowers another sample, as the #1700 sweep did.
3. If no safe option exists, document it as a known limitation (it already is in #1742) and close.

title: Flowchart layout: follow mermaid 12's ELK defaults (sibling-subgraph order, feedback edges)
author: dfadler
body:
Found while investigating #1834. Mermaid 12.0.0 made ELK the default layout engine for flowcharts (release notes: https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/releases/tag/mermaid%4012.0.0). mermaid.live renders the same: Nested Subgraphs there puts `A` left of `C`, matching `mermaid@12.1.0` headless, not 11.17.2 or our output.

Two things in `packages/svg-renderer/src/layout-engine/to-elk.ts` were written to imitate mermaid's old dagre layout (11.x) and now disagree with the reference:

1. **Sibling subgraphs are added in reverse declaration order** (`mermaidToElk` and `subgraphToElk`, issue #444). Mermaid 12's ELK graph puts them in source order when an edge ties them together. Nested Subgraphs: mermaid 12 has `A` at x=56, `C` at x=306; ours has `A` at 267, `C` at 72 (horizontal 20%). Note `Subgraphs` and `Nested Subgraphs (RL/BT)` still score 100%, so a change must keep those.
2. **Depth-first back edges are pre-reversed** (`edgesReversedForLayout`, #1307) to mimic dagre cycle breaking. Mermaid 12 uses ELK with `cycleBreaking: DEPTH_FIRST` and no `considerModelOrder`, and 12.1.0 adds `elk.orientFeedbackEdges` (on by default): an edge that points back into a subgraph from outside is flipped, so the subgraph stays contiguous. CI/CD Pipeline: mermaid 12 puts `D` (Fix & Retry) beside `C`; ours puts it at the bottom, below `F` (horizontal 48%, vertical 86%).

## Measured

`pnpm run layout:oracle`, mermaid 12.1.0: Nested Subgraphs 100% / 20%, CI/CD Pipeline 86% / 48%. With `layout: dagre, look: classic` on the same 12.1.0 both are 100/100 and 95/76, so the drop is the engine, not the version.

## What I tried (not committed)

- `considerModelOrder: NONE` and/or `cycleBreaking: DEPTH_FIRST` globally: no help for these two, and breaks ten other samples (Parallel Links, Text-Embedded Labels, System Architecture, ...). Model order must stay.
- Flipping both sibling-subgraph reversals to forward order: Nested Subgraphs stayed at 20%, so the ordering is decided somewhere else too (hop edges, ports or `compound-flat.ts` have not been checked).

## Suggested work

1. Find what decides sibling-subgraph left-right order for `E --> A`, `E --> C` into two sibling subgraphs, and make it source order for a flowchart (mermaid 12) without moving `Subgraphs` / `Nested Subgraphs (RL/BT)`.
2. Evaluate an `orientFeedbackEdges` equivalent: flip a cross-boundary edge that points back into a subgraph.
3. Score all four oracle types before and after; reject any option that lowers another sample. Check the GitHub render of the CI/CD sample before building (CLAUDE.md, "Parity with mermaid.js"); only mermaid.live was checked here.

title: ASCII: dense duplicate-edge graph keeps one closed stroke rectangle from unavoidable lane crossings
author: dfadler
body:
Left over from [#2040](https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/pull/2040).

## Problem

In a dense graph of duplicate edges, two lane crossings are unavoidable, so the output keeps one closed stroke rectangle (a ┼ crossing reads as a box).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["a"]
  b["b"]
  c["c"]
  a --> b
  a --> b
  a --> b
  a --> b
  b --> c
  b --> c
  a --> c
  a --> c
  c --> a
  c --> a
```

Current ASCII (TD): `a --> c` takes the only gutter column next to `b`, so the short `b`-side lanes cross it.

```
┌───────┐              
│       ├───────────┐  
│   a   ├─────┐     │  
│       │◄──┐ │     │  
└──┬─┬──┘   │ │     │  
   │ │      │ │     │  
   │ │      │ │     │  
   │ └────┐ │ │     │  
   │      │ │ │     │  
   ▼      │ │ │     │  
┌───────┐ │ │ │     │  
│       │◄┼─┼─┘     │  
│   b   │ │ │       │  
│       ├─┼─┼─┐     │  
└───┬───┘ │ │ │     │  
    │     │ │ │     │  
    │     │ │ │     │  
    │ ┌───┘ │ │     │  
    │ │     │ │     │  
    ▼ ▼     │ │     │  
┌───────┐   │ │     │  
│       ├───┘ │     │  
│   c   │◄────┘     │  
│       │◄──────────┘
```

Lanes can only grow outward, so a lane that has to reach a node on the far side of a nearer lane's column must cross it. The case is recorded with this reason in the `CROSSINGS` list of `ascii-duplicate-edges-2025-2028-2030.test.ts`.

title: Deep dive: ASCII layout behavior and whether it should keep output within a bounded width
author: dfadler
body:
## Question

Has the ASCII layout deviated from expected behavior around keeping a diagram within a bounded width (the maintainer's recollection is something like 80 columns), adjusting edge paths so the output does not run past it? This is a hypothesis to test, not an established regression.

## What prompted it

The ER stack in [#1522 (comment)](https://github.com/dfadler/zombie-mermaid/issues/1522#issuecomment-6314102620) renders with an off-center lower entity and a jogging edge compared with GitHub's render (tracked separately in the ER defect issue filed alongside this one). That raised the broader question of what the ASCII layout is supposed to guarantee.

## Starting evidence

- A quick grep of `packages/ascii-renderer/src/*.ts` for `maxWidth`, `max_width`, `columns` and `80` found no output-width budget or wrapping option in the renderer. It may live elsewhere (CLI, MCP, site), or never have existed; this has not been traced.
- `scripts/ascii-terminal-capture.sh` sizes the recording terminal to the larger of 100x40 and the rendered size, and its docs note that 39 of the 90 catalog samples exceed a stock 80x24 terminal. So wide output is currently accepted, not constrained.

## Scope of the deep dive

1. Find out whether a width budget ever existed: search git history (`git log -S`) and closed issues/PRs for width, wrap, 80 columns or terminal-width handling.
2. Document what the layout currently guarantees per diagram type (flowchart, sequence, class, state, ER): spacing, alignment, edge routing rules, and what happens when output exceeds a terminal width.
3. Decide, with the maintainer, what the intended contract is (no width limit, a soft budget, or an option), and file follow-ups for any gap.

Findings go in this issue as comments, per the repo's research convention, not in a `docs/research/` file.

Related: #1917, #2076, #1592.

🤖 **Claude:** Findings for #2238. Research only; no code, baseline or issue touched. Checked against `origin/main` at bd0a701c.

## 1. Did a width budget ever exist?

Short answer: not in the default renderer, and never at the point the layout is computed. Three width mechanisms exist, all added later and all outside the grid layout:

| Mechanism | Where | Since | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-w/--max-width <n\|auto>` (CLI, `render --ascii`) | `src/cli.ts`, `src/cli/parse-args.ts`, `src/cli/render.ts` | #382 (`e22e76d2`, 2026-08-31), #335 | `auto` is `process.stdout.columns`, 80 outside a TTY. Warns on stderr when output is wider; stdout is never truncated. |
| Compact-spacing fallback for `-w` | `src/cli/render.ts` | `88199c14` (2026-09-04) | On overflow, retries once with the tightest node/border padding; prints the narrower diagram if it fits, else the full one plus the warning. Skipped when `-x/-y/-p` are already at or below compact. |
| `maxCols` (default `DEFAULT_MAX_COLS` = 120; `Infinity` disables) | `packages/ascii-layout/src/rasterize.ts`, only for opt-in `--layout mermaid` | #2181 (`e99c819e`), #2182 | Shrinks blank gaps between node groups; never scales boxes. If it cannot fit, falls back to the default renderer (`fallbackReason`), or keeps wide text with `mermaid-wide`. |

Also relevant: `profile: 'markdown'` (#1866) is about glyph safety (paste-safe, ASCII-only), not width.

History: `git log -S` for `maxWidth`/`columns`/`80 col` across `packages/ascii-renderer` and `src` finds nothing before #382, back to the initial import (`3185b9b6`, beautiful-mermaid v0.1.0). The only `maxWidth` in the renderer is `adjMaxWidth` in `sequence.ts`, a per-gap column width, not a budget. #335 (closed 2026-09-04) states the gap outright ("no way to cap it for a fixed-width terminal") and scoped the real fix, "label wrapping, direction flipping" as in AlexanderGrooff/mermaid-ascii#47, out as follow-up work that was not done. So the maintainer's 80-column recollection most likely traces to #335/#382 or to mermaid-ascii#47, not to a removed renderer behaviour. I found no commit that removed a budget. The `ascii-terminal-capture.sh` sizing (the larger of 100x40 and the output) is a capture detail, not a contract.

## 2. What the default layout guarantees today

Measured: `renderMermaidASCII(source, { colorMode: 'none' })` on every source in `packages/site/samples-data.ts` (the visual-test samples, 174 total, including 9 `%%{init}%%`-prefixed ones not broken out by type; not the 100 `xychart-N` gallery cases), widest line in code points, by first keyword:

| Type | n | median | max | >80 cols | >120 cols |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| flowchart | 27 | 37 | 68 | 0 | 0 |
| graph | 26 | 45 | 206 | 3 | 1 |
| stateDiagram-v2 | 8 | 32 | 60 | 0 | 0 |
| sequenceDiagram | 21 | 46 | 101 | 2 | 0 |
| classDiagram (+v2) | 28 | 32 | 101 | 2 | 0 |
| erDiagram | 20 | 23 | 97 | 1 | 0 |
| xychart | 10 | 72 | 130 | 3 | 1 |
| pie | 19 | 52 | 84 | 1 | 0 |
| architecture | 3 | 70 | 80 | 0 | 0 |
| C4 (3 types) | 3 | 38-65 | 65 | 0 | 0 |

Widest: "All 12 Flowchart Shapes" at 206 columns, then "XY: Numeric X-Axis" at 130. 12 of the 174 exceed 80 columns, 2 exceed 120. (The capture script docs say 39 of 90 catalog samples exceed 80x24; that is a different sample set and counts rows too, so the numbers do not compare.) The `graph` row mixes TD and LR sources.

Guarantee, in practice: every diagram renders at its natural width; spacing (`-x/-y/-p`, `paddingX/paddingY/boxBorderPadding`) is the only user-visible knob, there is no render-time budget, no wrapping of long lines or labels, and no direction flipping. Width is bounded only by the diagram's own size. What each family does to shrink or grow is by design per type: sequence widens gaps to fit message labels (`adjMaxWidth`), class and ER grow boxes to their longest member, and labels on vertical edges sit beside the stroke (#1284/#1332), which adds width.

## 3. The ER stack that prompted this

Not a width issue. The off-centre lower entity and the jogging edge in #1522 are placement and routing, which `#1592`'s ER deep dive already records (general-75/77 ASCII baselines) and which the ER defect issue filed alongside #2238 tracks. Whether a width cap would change them is untested.

## 4. Where the gaps are, and the decision needed

The contract today is "no limit, plus a CLI warning and one compaction retry". Gaps against what the issue asks:

1. **Library and MCP callers get nothing.** `-w` exists only in the CLI. `renderMermaidASCII` has no `maxWidth` option, and the MCP tool has no equivalent, so the one place an agent would hit a width problem is the one with no help. (MCP: not checked beyond the absence of any `maxWidth` hit in `git grep`.)
2. **Compaction is a single retry** of padding values; nothing is wrapped, flipped or re-routed. A 206-column diagram cannot be brought to 80 columns this way (a direction flip to TD is what mermaid-ascii#47 does).
3. **`--layout mermaid` has a cap, the default renderer does not.** The same diagram can be bounded in one mode and unbounded in the other; the cap in the opt-in mode silently relies on falling back to the unbounded renderer when it fails.

This is the maintainer's call, so I am not filing issues for it. The options, smallest first: (a) keep "no limit" and document it plus `-w` in `docs/diagrams.md` (`-w` is mentioned only in the CLI help and, for the opt-in mode, `docs/known-differences.md`; not in the per-diagram guides); (b) promote the compaction retry into a library option (`maxWidth`, reuse the CLI logic) and report whether it fit; (c) add the mermaid-ascii#47 cascade (label wrapping, direction flip for LR to TD). I would pick (a) now and (b) if library or MCP users ask. Tell me which and I will file it.

**Not checked:** the MCP server's ASCII path in detail; the 100 `xychart-N` ASCII cases; real-terminal wrapping behaviour (no PTY capture); whether `profile: 'markdown'` changes widths.
